newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Foreign investment in Pakistan stocks seen down.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Pakistan stocks seen down.

text.p: Foreign investment in Pakistani stocks is likely to slide in the coming months after the collapse of an IMF standby loan, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The initial reaction of overseas funds regarding this news is negative. We should forget about the inflow of any new money from foreigners for the next few months," said Sameer Ahmed, chief dealer of ING Baring Securities.
"Overseas investors look for the IMF's seal of approval for government policies which is not there now. Only dedicated funds for Pakistan will maintain their positions," Ahmed said.

The International Monetary Fund, unable to proceed with the standby loan due to Pakistan's failure to meet targets, has agreed to continue monitoring the economy and possibly start talks on a softer, medium-term loan later in the year.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif is expected to announce major economic reforms in the next day or two that are expected to include many measures long sought by the IMF and World Bank.
Analysts said overseas investors were already wary because of Pakistan's weak economic fundamentals and the effective suspension of the standby loan would deter fresh inflows.
"Foreigners have pulled back their orders after the IMF halted its standby arrangement with Pakistan and blue chips are under pressure," said analyst Shoaib Memon of Carr Mashriq.
The Karachi Stock Exchange said foreign investors had sold 42.71 million rupees ($1.06 million) of shares in the past month while buying shares worth only 21.12 million rupees.
Memon said local players were propping up the index on hopes of a business-friendly economic package, but could not do so for long in the absence of foreign and institutional support.

However, Farooq Lakhani, country manager of International Asset Management Company, said the interruption in IMF lending would not hit the market too hard because the government had no immediate liquidity problem and foreign investors had already reduced their exposure to Pakistan.
"There won't be much impact...as the inflow of foreign funds is already limited. Only the funds which believe in the country in the long term are here," he said.
"I think the IMF action was premature. It did not give the new government enough time to settle in and insisted on the past contract which was difficult to meet at this stage.

"I won't say the IMF's conditions, including a cut in the budget deficit, an increase in revenue collection and curtailment in administrative expenditure, are wrong, but the fund tried to rush things," he said.
"The new government, which enjoys a big mandate, should have been allowed to make economic reforms," he added.
On Tuesday the Karachi 100-share index rose 10.31 points, or 0.65 percent, to 1,588.47 on expectations for Sharif's policy speech.
